claims.text: Applying a TiN surface coating to boride-based components will improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
The TiN coating forms a chemically inert barrier between the boride substrate and molten aluminum.
Preventing direct contact between the boride substrate and molten aluminum reduces corrosion.
FeB, CrB, and WB are candidate boride-based component materials for hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment.
A thin, uniform TiN coating can be deposited on the component by physical vapor deposition.
Temperatures of 650–700°C are typical of hot-dip aluminum-plating exposure.
The coating is expected to remain protective under periodic thermal cycling and mechanical abrasion associated with industrial operation.
TiN acts as a diffusion barrier that prevents aluminum from reacting with the underlying boride phase.
Blocking aluminum diffusion and reaction inhibits interfacial corrosion.
TiN is chemically stable and inert in contact with molten aluminum at high temperatures.
TiN's high hardness and low wettability reduce aluminum adhesion and penetration.
Reduced aluminum adhesion and penetration limit intermetallic-compound formation and corrosive attack on the boride substrate.
TiN-coated boride components will have lower mass loss, less surface degradation, and longer service life than uncoated boride components under identical exposure.
TiN coating will reduce the corrosion rate by a factor of 2–5 relative to an uncoated-boride baseline.
Damage to the TiN coating will diminish its effectiveness.
A TiN coating thinner than 1 μm may have diminished effectiveness.
Operation above 800°C may exceed TiN's thermal stability and diminish coating effectiveness.
The magnitude of improvement may depend on coating quality and the particular boride substrate.
